Its wall has three layers: an outer serosa, a thick middle myometrium of smooth muscle, and the inner endometrium. The endometrium is the layer that matters cyclically. It is itself divided into a superficial functional layer, or functionalis, which grows and is shed each cycle, and a deeper basal layer, the basalis, which is never shed and which regenerates the functionalis afterwards. This division explains why menstruation is a controlled, self-limiting process rather than an open wound.

The blood supply to the endometrium is unusual and deliberately fragile. Spiral arterioles — coiled vessels that grow up through the functionalis as it thickens — are exquisitely sensitive to hormonal signals and are the structures whose constriction initiates a period.

At the lower end, the cervix is a firm cylinder of dense connective tissue about 2.5 to 3 centimetres long, forming the neck of the uterus. Its canal is lined by glands producing mucus whose quantity, viscosity and molecular architecture change dramatically across the cycle, functioning as a hormone-controlled gate that is closed to sperm for most of the month and open for a few days.

sections.heading: The Control System: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian Axis
sections.body:
The cycle is governed by a three-level hormonal circuit conventionally called the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Understanding it as a control loop, rather than as a list of chemicals, makes almost everything else follow logically.

At the top sits the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain, which releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH. The crucial feature of GnRH is that it is secreted in pulses, not continuously. A burst is released roughly every 60 to 90 minutes during the first half of the cycle and slows to roughly every three to four hours in the second half. This pulsatility is not a quirk; it is essential. If GnRH is delivered continuously rather than in pulses, the pituitary desensitises and shuts down within days — a fact exploited medically by GnRH agonist drugs used to suppress the cycle in endometriosis and some cancers.

The pulses travel a short distance through a dedicated portal blood system to the anterior pituitary gland, which responds by releasing two gonadotropins: follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH, and luteinising hormone, LH. Faster GnRH pulses favour LH release; slower pulses favour FSH. This frequency coding is how one upstream hormone controls the ratio of two downstream ones.

FSH and LH travel in the general circulation to the ovary. FSH, as its name suggests, drives the growth of ovarian follicles and stimulates the granulosa cells surrounding each egg to convert androgens into oestradiol, the principal and most potent oestrogen. LH acts primarily on the outer theca cells to produce those androgen precursors, and later triggers ovulation and sustains the structure left behind. This division of labour is called the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model and it explains why both hormones are necessary.

The ovary then reports back. Oestradiol, progesterone and the peptide hormones inhibin A and inhibin B feed back to the hypothalamus and pituitary. For most of the cycle this feedback is negative: rising oestradiol suppresses FSH, which limits how many follicles can develop. But the system contains one remarkable switch. When oestradiol exceeds roughly 200 picograms per millilitre (about 730 picomoles per litre) and stays there for something like 36 to 48 hours, the feedback flips from negative to positive, and high oestradiol now drives a massive release of LH instead of suppressing it. That switch is what causes ovulation, and it is the single most elegant feature of the whole system.

Because the loop runs through the brain, it is exposed to everything the brain is exposed to. Severe energy deficit, extreme exercise loads, acute illness, major psychological stress and disrupted sleep can all slow or silence GnRH pulses, which is why the cycle is such a sensitive indicator of general physiological state.

sections.heading: The Follicular Phase: Recruitment, Selection and the Dominant Follicle
sections.body:
By convention the cycle is numbered from the first day of full menstrual bleeding, which is day one. The follicular phase runs from there until ovulation, and it is the variable half of the cycle: in an adult it may last anywhere from about ten days to three weeks, and nearly all the difference between a short cycle and a long one lives here.

The phase actually begins before the previous period ends. As the corpus luteum from the last cycle dies, progesterone, oestradiol and inhibin A all fall, and their combined negative feedback lifts. FSH rises modestly in the last few days of the preceding luteal phase and the first few days of bleeding. This intercycle FSH rise is the recruitment signal. A cohort of small antral follicles — typically five to twenty per ovary, each two to ten millimetres across and each containing one egg arrested in mid-division since before the woman was born — is rescued from the atresia that would otherwise consume them.

What follows is a competition. Each recruited follicle has a slightly different sensitivity to FSH, determined by how many FSH receptors its granulosa cells carry. As the follicles grow, they collectively produce more oestradiol and inhibin B, and these suppress pituitary FSH. Circulating FSH therefore falls just as the follicles are becoming more dependent on it. The one follicle that happened to be marginally ahead — the one with the lowest FSH threshold — can continue growing in the now-scarce hormone, while its rivals fall below their own thresholds and undergo atresia. By roughly day seven, a single dominant follicle has been selected, a process sometimes described as selection by deprivation. It reaches about 18 to 24 millimetres in diameter by ovulation and is then called a Graafian follicle.

The dominant follicle also secures its own future by switching hormone sensitivity. Under continued oestradiol exposure, its granulosa cells begin expressing LH receptors, so that as FSH declines it can respond to LH instead. Fluid accumulates in a central cavity, the antrum, and the egg sits on a mound of cells at one edge.

Meanwhile the follicle's oestradiol output climbs steeply, from perhaps 40 picograms per millilitre early in the phase to 200 to 400 by the day before ovulation. That oestradiol has three visible consequences elsewhere. It drives the endometrium to regenerate and thicken from about one millimetre after menstruation to eight to twelve millimetres, with straight tubular glands and new blood vessels — the proliferative phase. It changes cervical mucus from scant and tacky to copious, clear and stretchy. And it produces the psychological and physical texture many people recognise as the better half of the month: comparatively stable mood, rising energy and libido, and few physical symptoms.

sections.heading: Ovulation: The LH Surge and the Release of the Egg
sections.body:
Ovulation is a brief, violent and precisely timed event, and it is triggered by the feedback switch described earlier. Once circulating oestradiol has been sustained above roughly 200 picograms per millilitre for something on the order of 36 to 48 hours, the hypothalamus and pituitary reverse their response: instead of suppressing gonadotropins, high oestradiol now provokes an enormous release of LH. Serum LH rises roughly tenfold over a few hours, with a smaller concurrent FSH rise. The whole surge lasts about 48 hours from onset to return to baseline.

The timings within that window matter for anyone trying to conceive or avoid conception. Ovulation typically occurs about 24 to 36 hours after the onset of the LH surge, and about 10 to 12 hours after the LH peak. Home ovulation predictor kits detect LH in urine and generally turn positive at surge onset, which is why the standard advice is that the fertile days are the day of the first positive test and the two days following.

At the ovary, LH sets off a cascade that is best understood as a controlled inflammatory rupture. The egg, arrested since fetal life in the first meiotic division, resumes meiosis and completes it to the point of extruding a first polar body, leaving it arrested again at metaphase of the second division, where it will remain unless fertilised. The cells binding the egg to the follicle wall loosen as they secrete hyaluronic acid, producing an expanded, sticky cumulus mass. Simultaneously the follicle wall is digested from within: prostaglandins, proteolytic enzymes including plasmin and matrix metalloproteinases, and local vascular changes weaken a small area of the ovarian surface until it gives way. The follicle does not explode; it opens, and the egg with its surrounding cumulus cells is released and swept up by the fimbriae of the fallopian tube.

Roughly a fifth of people can feel this. Mittelschmerz — German for "middle pain" — is a one-sided lower abdominal ache or twinge lasting minutes to a day or so, thought to arise from follicular distension, the small amount of blood and follicular fluid released into the peritoneal cavity, or tubal contraction. It is normal, though it is not a reliable timing marker because it can precede or follow the actual release.

The egg is short-lived. It remains fertilisable for approximately 12 to 24 hours after release, and if not fertilised it degenerates. Sperm, by contrast, can survive up to about five days in the receptive cervical mucus present around ovulation. The asymmetry between those two survival times is what defines the fertile window, and it is why intercourse before ovulation matters far more than intercourse after it.

sections.heading: The Luteal Phase: The Corpus Luteum and the Reign of Progesterone
sections.body:
After the egg leaves, the collapsed follicle does not simply disappear. Under the influence of LH, its remaining granulosa and theca cells undergo a dramatic transformation called luteinisation: they enlarge, fill with lipid droplets and a yellow pigment that gives the structure its name, and become a temporary endocrine gland, the corpus luteum, roughly two centimetres across. It is one of the very few endocrine organs in the human body that is built and destroyed on a schedule.

The corpus luteum's principal product is progesterone, secreted at 20 to 40 milligrams per day at peak, alongside oestradiol and inhibin A. Serum progesterone rises from under 1 nanogram per millilitre before ovulation to a mid-luteal peak of typically 10 to 20 nanograms per millilitre about seven days after ovulation. A mid-luteal progesterone above roughly 3 nanograms per millilitre is the standard laboratory confirmation that ovulation actually occurred.

Progesterone's job is to convert the oestrogen-primed endometrium into tissue capable of supporting an implanting embryo. The straight proliferative glands become coiled and tortuous and begin secreting glycogen-rich fluid; the stroma swells and its cells transform in a process called decidualisation; spiral arterioles coil more tightly. This is the secretory phase. There is a narrow interval, roughly days 20 to 24 of an idealised cycle or about six to ten days after ovulation, during which the lining is receptive to implantation — the so-called window of implantation. Outside it, even a healthy embryo generally cannot attach.

Progesterone also acts systemically, and these effects explain most of what people notice in the second half of the month. It raises the hypothalamic temperature set point, producing a sustained basal body temperature rise of about 0.2 to 0.5 degrees Celsius that persists until it withdraws. It thickens cervical mucus into an impenetrable plug. It relaxes smooth muscle, slowing gut transit and contributing to bloating and constipation. Its metabolite allopregnanolone acts on GABA-A receptors in the brain, which for most people is calming and mildly sedating but which in a minority appears to produce the opposite, and is a leading candidate explanation for premenstrual mood disorders.

The luteal phase is notably consistent in length — typically 11 to 17 days, most often 12 to 14 — because the corpus luteum has a fixed intrinsic lifespan of about 14 days unless rescued. If no pregnancy occurs, it undergoes programmed regression, luteolysis, and progesterone and oestradiol collapse over two to three days. If an embryo does implant, its trophoblast secretes human chorionic gonadotropin, hCG, which is structurally similar enough to LH to bind the same receptor and keep the corpus luteum alive until the placenta takes over hormone production at around seven to nine weeks.

sections.heading: Menstruation: What the Bleed Actually Is and How It Stops Itself
sections.body:
A period is not a passive leak. It is an actively orchestrated, tightly controlled demolition of a tissue that the body built a fortnight earlier, and understanding it as such explains almost every feature people notice about it.

The trigger is withdrawal, not presence. When the corpus luteum regresses and progesterone falls from mid-luteal levels to near zero over about two to three days, the endometrium loses the signal that was holding it stable. Lysosomes within the stromal cells become leaky, releasing enzymes; matrix metalloproteinases that were suppressed by progesterone are switched on and begin digesting the collagen scaffolding of the functional layer; and inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils and macrophages, flood in. Prostaglandins, especially prostaglandin F2-alpha, are synthesised in large quantities. These cause intense constriction of the spiral arterioles, so the outer endometrium is starved of blood and dies, and they also cause the myometrium to contract, expelling the shed material.

Bleeding follows when the constricted vessels relax and the damaged, enzyme-weakened tissue breaks away. Menstrual fluid is therefore not pure blood: roughly half to two-thirds by volume is blood, and the remainder is endometrial tissue fragments, cervical and vaginal secretions, inflammatory cells and enzymes. It contains fibrinolytic enzymes, notably plasmin, that deliberately dissolve clots so the fluid can leave the uterus — which is why menstrual blood usually does not clot in the way a cut does, and why visible clots suggest bleeding fast enough to outrun that mechanism.

Haemostasis, the stopping of bleeding, happens by three overlapping means. Continued vasoconstriction limits flow; platelet plugs and fibrin form at the torn vessel ends; and, most distinctively, the endometrium regenerates with extraordinary speed. Under rising oestradiol from the next cohort of follicles, epithelium spreads across the raw surface from the intact basal layer and from gland stumps, resurfacing the cavity within about 48 hours of the flow beginning — scarless healing of a kind seen almost nowhere else in the adult body.

The numbers are worth knowing because they anchor judgements about what is normal. Bleeding lasts typically three to eight days, with the heaviest flow almost always in the first two. Total blood loss has a median of about 30 to 40 millilitres per period, roughly two to three tablespoons; total menstrual fluid is perhaps twice that. Losses above 80 millilitres are the classical research definition of heavy menstrual bleeding, though modern clinical practice sensibly defines it by impact on the person rather than by measurement.

Prostaglandins also explain the associated symptoms. Because they act on smooth muscle generally and are absorbed into the circulation, they cause not only uterine cramping but also the diarrhoea, nausea, headache and faintness that many people experience on the first day. This is exactly why non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which block prostaglandin synthesis, are more effective for period pain than simple analgesics like paracetamol.

sections.heading: What Counts as Normal: Length, Flow, Variation and Regularity
sections.body:
Almost every diagram of the menstrual cycle shows twenty-eight days, and this has caused enormous unnecessary anxiety. Twenty-eight is a convenient average, not a target. Large prospective studies of hundreds of thousands of cycles put the population median nearer 29 days, and, critically, show that only a small minority of individual cycles are exactly 28 days long.

The current international standard, from the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, defines normal cycle length in adults as 24 to 38 days measured from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Shorter than 24 days is polymenorrhoea; longer than 38 is oligomenorrhoea. Within-person variation matters as much as the average: normal is variation of less than seven to nine days between the shortest and longest cycle over a year. Someone whose cycles run 26, 34, 27 and 40 days has a regularity problem even though every individual cycle falls inside the range.

Normal bleeding duration is up to eight days. Normal volume is defined functionally: bleeding that does not interfere with physical, social, emotional or material quality of life. Practical markers of excess include soaking through a pad or tampon in an hour for several consecutive hours, needing double protection, regularly changing protection overnight, passing clots larger than about 2.5 centimetres, and iron deficiency without another explanation. Practical markers of unusually light bleeding include spotting only, or bleeding lasting under two days, which can signal a thin endometrium, intrauterine scarring, or anovulation.

The two variable and fixed halves of the cycle explain most confusion. The luteal phase, from ovulation to menstruation, is quite fixed at 11 to 17 days because the corpus luteum has a set lifespan. The follicular phase absorbs almost all the variability. A person with 34-day cycles is not carrying an extra week of luteal phase; they are taking longer to select and mature a dominant follicle. This has a practical corollary: ovulation is not on day 14 in anyone but a 28-day cycler, and estimating it as "cycle length minus 14" is a far better rule than assuming mid-cycle.

Age reshapes the picture predictably. Cycles are longest and most erratic in the first two to three years after menarche, when many are anovulatory; they shorten and stabilise through the twenties and thirties, often reaching their most regular around ages 25 to 40; then they shorten further in the early forties before becoming erratic in perimenopause. Occasional anovulatory cycles happen to almost everyone, and a single unusual cycle after illness, travel, sleep disruption or a stressful month is rarely significant. A persistent change in pattern over three or more cycles is the thing worth investigating.

sections.heading: Tracking a Cycle Accurately: Calendar, Temperature, Mucus and Tests
sections.body:
Cycle tracking done properly gives real information; done casually it gives false confidence. The three classical signs each measure something different, and their weaknesses are complementary, which is why combined or symptothermal methods substantially outperform any single one. Calendar records establish your personal length and variability but predict ovulation only retrospectively and poorly. Basal body temperature confirms ovulation but only after the fact. Cervical mucus predicts ovulation prospectively but is subjective. Urinary LH tests bracket ovulation within a day or two but say nothing about whether the egg was actually released.

Two practical cautions apply before starting. First, tracking requires several months of data before it means anything; a single charted cycle establishes almost nothing, and three to six are needed to see a personal pattern. Second, the signs are degraded by specific circumstances: fever, alcohol, shift work and broken sleep all disturb basal temperature, while semen, lubricants, spermicides, vaginal infections and some medications alter or mask cervical mucus. Record those disturbances alongside the readings rather than discarding them, since an unexplained gap in a chart is far harder to interpret later than an annotated one.
steps: Record the calendar. Log day one as the first day of proper bleeding, not spotting. After three to six cycles you will have your own range, from which the shortest and longest cycle define your personal variability.

Take basal body temperature on waking. Use a thermometer reading to two decimal places, measure at the same time each morning after at least three hours of continuous sleep, before sitting up, drinking or speaking, and use the same site (oral, vaginal or rectal) throughout. Record even disturbed readings, marked as such.

Identify the thermal shift. Ovulation has occurred when three consecutive readings sit at least 0.2 degrees Celsius above the highest of the preceding six. The rise happens one to three days after ovulation, so temperature confirms but never predicts.

Observe cervical mucus daily. After menstruation there is typically a dry or scant phase, then thick and tacky white or cream secretions, then, as oestradiol peaks, clear, slippery, stretchy mucus resembling raw egg white which can be drawn several centimetres between the fingers. The last day of that slippery quality — the peak day — is the closest single marker to ovulation.
Optionally check cervical position. Under high oestradiol the cervix rises, softens and its opening widens slightly; afterwards it drops, firms and closes.

Use urinary LH tests if precision matters. Test once or twice daily starting about five days before the earliest ovulation your calendar suggests. A positive marks surge onset, with ovulation usually 24 to 36 hours later.

Cross-check with the luteal phase length. Count from the confirmed thermal shift to the next period. Consistently fewer than ten days may indicate a luteal phase defect and is worth discussing with a clinician.

Treat app predictions with suspicion. Most apps extrapolate from calendar averages and will confidently show a fertile window that your own temperature and mucus data contradict. Your observations outrank the algorithm.

sections.heading: Fertility, the Fertile Window and How Conception Actually Works
sections.body:
The fertile window is defined by an asymmetry. The egg survives roughly 12 to 24 hours after ovulation, while sperm can survive up to about five days within the crypts of the cervix when oestrogen-dominant mucus is present. Combining these gives a window of about six days: the five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation itself. Probability of conception is not flat across it; large prospective studies place the highest per-act probability in the two days immediately preceding ovulation and on ovulation day itself, with essentially zero chance from the day after ovulation until the next cycle.

Cervical mucus is the gate. For most of the cycle, progesterone-influenced mucus is thick, acidic and structurally a dense mesh that sperm cannot penetrate. Under peak oestradiol it becomes abundant, watery, alkaline and organised into parallel channels that both filter abnormal sperm and conduct normal ones upward. Sperm are also stored temporarily in cervical crypts and released over the following days, which is the mechanism behind the five-day survival figure.

Of the 100 to 300 million sperm in a typical ejaculate, only a few hundred reach the outer third of the fallopian tube where fertilisation occurs, four to six hours later. They must undergo capacitation, a biochemical maturation in the female tract that makes them capable of fertilising at all. When one penetrates the egg's outer coat, the zona pellucida, the egg completes its second meiotic division and mounts a rapid block to further sperm entry.

The fertilised egg then divides as it travels down the tube, reaching the uterus as a 16-to-32-cell morula around day three or four and becoming a blastocyst by day five. Implantation occurs six to ten days after ovulation, most commonly on days eight to ten, and hCG becomes detectable in blood within a day or two of that, and in urine a few days later. This is why testing before a missed period frequently gives a false negative: the pregnancy may be real but the hormone has not yet accumulated.

Realistic expectations matter. For a couple in their twenties with no fertility problems, the chance of conception in any single cycle with well-timed intercourse is roughly 20 to 30 percent; about 85 percent conceive within twelve months. Fecundity declines gradually from the early thirties and more steeply after 37. Clinical guidance in most countries is to investigate after twelve months of trying under age 35, and after six months at 35 or over, or sooner if cycles are irregular or there is known pelvic pathology.

Finally, natural family planning used for contraception has a substantial failure rate — perfect-use figures for symptothermal methods are low, but typical-use failure rates commonly reported are around 2 to 23 percent per year depending on method and adherence.

sections.heading: Menarche and the Adolescent Years: Why Early Cycles Are Erratic
sections.body:
The first period, menarche, occurs at a median age of about 12 to 13 years in well-nourished populations, with a normal range of roughly 9 to 15. It is not the beginning of puberty but a comparatively late milestone within it, typically arriving two to three years after breast budding and usually within a year after the peak of the adolescent growth spurt. Because of that ordering, a girl who has begun breast development is usually within a predictable window, and menarche after age 15, or absence of any breast development by 13, warrants assessment.

Timing is set by a combination of genetics, nutrition and body composition. Menarche has advanced by several years across the past two centuries in industrialised countries, an effect attributed mainly to improved childhood nutrition and reduced infectious disease burden, and the trend appears to have largely plateaued in high-income settings while continuing in others. Leptin, a hormone produced by fat tissue, appears to act as a permissive signal to the hypothalamus, which is part of why very low body fat delays menarche and why chronic energy deficit can stop cycles at any age.

The crucial physiological point about adolescence is that the positive-feedback switch — the mechanism whereby sustained high oestradiol triggers an LH surge — matures later than the rest of the axis. Follicles grow and produce oestrogen, and the endometrium proliferates and eventually sheds, but ovulation may not occur. The result is anovulatory cycles: irregular, unpredictable, often long, and sometimes heavy, because an endometrium built by unopposed oestrogen with no progesterone to organise and stabilise it sheds patchily and incompletely.

This is normal and self-correcting. In the first year after menarche, roughly half or more of cycles are anovulatory; by three years out, most are ovulatory, and by five years the pattern generally resembles the adult one. Guidance from paediatric and gynaecological bodies accordingly treats cycles in the first year or two as normal if they fall anywhere between about 21 and 45 days.

Certain patterns, however, should not be dismissed as teenage irregularity. Cycles consistently shorter than 21 days or longer than 45 after the second year; no period for 90 days at any point; bleeding requiring hourly protection changes, especially from the very first period, which can unmask an inherited bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease; and pain severe enough to cause repeated school absence are all reasons to seek assessment rather than to wait.

Practically, adolescents benefit enormously from being taught what to record and what the ranges are, from having supplies and analgesia available before they are needed, and from being told explicitly that severe pain is a medical complaint rather than a rite of passage. Reassurance about irregularity should be given alongside the specific thresholds at which irregularity stops being expected.

sections.heading: Perimenopause and Menopause: The Long Tail of the Cycle
sections.body:
Menopause is defined retrospectively as twelve consecutive months without a period in the absence of another cause. The median age is around 51 in most studied populations, with a normal range of roughly 45 to 55. Menopause before 40 is termed premature ovarian insufficiency and affects about 1 percent of women; between 40 and 45 it is described as early menopause. Both warrant medical assessment, partly because the associated oestrogen deficiency carries long-term bone and cardiovascular consequences that are usually treated.

The transition to it, perimenopause, typically begins in the mid-forties and lasts on average about four years, though a range of a few months to more than ten years is well documented. Its driver is the exhaustion of the follicle pool. As the number of remaining antral follicles falls, so does their output of inhibin B, and because inhibin B is a principal brake on pituitary FSH, FSH rises. Higher FSH recruits and matures the remaining follicles faster, which is why the earliest reliable sign of perimenopause is usually cycle shortening — periods arriving every 24 or 25 days rather than 29.

What follows is characteristically erratic rather than a smooth decline. Oestradiol in early perimenopause is frequently higher and more volatile than in younger women, not lower, because the accelerated follicular development produces surges. This explains the paradox that many people experience heavier bleeding, worse breast tenderness and more pronounced premenstrual symptoms during a phase they had expected to be one of oestrogen deficiency. Anovulatory cycles become common, and because progesterone is then absent, the endometrium can grow thick and shed unpredictably. Later perimenopause is marked by skipped periods, gaps of 60 days or more, and eventually cessation.

Symptoms arise mostly from oestradiol instability and withdrawal. Vasomotor symptoms — hot flushes and night sweats — affect perhaps 60 to 80 percent of women at some point and are now understood to involve KNDy neurons in the hypothalamus that lose oestrogen restraint and destabilise the thermoregulatory set point. Sleep disruption, mood changes, joint aches, urogenital dryness and cognitive fogginess are common. Bone loss accelerates around the final menstrual period, with the fastest loss in the year before and two years after.

Two practical points are frequently missed. First, contraception is still required: ovulation continues intermittently and unpredictably, and pregnancy remains possible until twelve months of amenorrhoea after age 50, or twenty-four months under 50. Second, any bleeding after menopause has been established is abnormal and should be investigated promptly, because although most causes are benign — usually atrophy of the lining — a minority represent endometrial cancer, and it is highly treatable when found early.

A related point concerns what perimenopause is not. Because its symptoms overlap heavily with those of thyroid disease, depression, anaemia, sleep apnoea and simple overwork, attributing everything to hormones in a woman in her forties is a recognised source of missed diagnoses. Equally, FSH testing is of limited value during the transition, because levels fluctuate wildly from week to week; a single normal result does not exclude perimenopause and a single raised one does not confirm menopause.

sections.heading: Cyclical Symptoms: Cramps, Premenstrual Change and What Is Treatable
sections.body:
Period pain, or dysmenorrhoea, comes in two forms with different implications. Primary dysmenorrhoea is pain without underlying pelvic disease, typically starting within a year or two of menarche once ovulatory cycles are established, beginning a few hours before or with the flow and lasting one to three days. Its cause is well established: prostaglandin F2-alpha, released as the endometrium breaks down, drives intense uterine contractions with pressures that can exceed 150 to 200 millimetres of mercury, transiently cutting uterine blood supply and producing ischaemic pain of the same character as angina. Concentrations of these prostaglandins measure roughly two to four times higher in people with severe cramps.

Secondary dysmenorrhoea is pain caused by an identifiable condition — endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, pelvic infection or an intrauterine device. Its distinguishing features are onset years after menarche, pain that begins several days before bleeding or persists after it, worsening over time, deep pain during sex, and poor response to standard treatment. Those features are the reason to seek investigation rather than stronger painkillers.

Treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea is genuinely effective and underused. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block the enzyme that makes prostaglandins and relieve pain in roughly 70 to 80 percent of cases; they work far better when started at the first twinge or up to a day before the expected period, because they prevent prostaglandin synthesis rather than reversing its effects. Typical regimens are ibuprofen 400 milligrams every six to eight hours or naproxen 500 milligrams initially then 250 every six to eight hours, taken with food, avoided in those with peptic ulcer disease, kidney impairment or aspirin-sensitive asthma. Heat applied to the lower abdomen at around 40 degrees Celsius has been shown in trials to be roughly comparable to ibuprofen. Combined hormonal contraception, which thins the endometrium and reduces prostaglandin production, is the standard second line.

Premenstrual symptoms are a separate phenomenon, arising in the luteal phase and resolving within a few days of bleeding starting. Mild cyclical changes in mood, appetite, breast comfort, bloating and sleep are near-universal. Premenstrual syndrome, meaning symptoms severe enough to impair functioning, affects perhaps 20 to 30 percent. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a formal psychiatric diagnosis, affects around 3 to 8 percent and involves marked mood disturbance, irritability or hopelessness confined to the luteal phase.

The mechanism is not simply "too much" or "too little" of a hormone; measured levels in affected and unaffected people are largely similar. The leading hypothesis is differential sensitivity to normal fluctuations, particularly to allopregnanolone, a progesterone metabolite acting on GABA-A receptors. Evidence supports SSRIs, which often work within days rather than weeks and can be taken luteal-phase only, ovulation suppression, and, more modestly, exercise and calcium supplementation.

sections.heading: Managing the Bleed: Products, Hygiene and Practical Supplies
sections.body:
Menstrual products divide into absorbent items worn externally, absorbent items worn internally, and collection devices. Each has different capacity, wear time and risk profile, and there is no single best choice; the sensible approach is to keep more than one type available, because heavy days, travel, sleep and limited washing facilities all favour different solutions. Capacity is worth knowing in real terms: a regular tampon absorbs about 5 millilitres, a super about 9 to 12, a typical day pad about 10 to 15, and a menstrual cup holds about 20 to 30, which is most of an entire average period.

Wear times are safety limits, not suggestions. Tampons and internal sponges should be changed at least every four to eight hours and never left beyond eight, because prolonged use is the main modifiable risk factor for menstrual toxic shock syndrome, a rare but rapidly progressive illness caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus, with an incidence usually quoted around one per 100,000 menstruating people per year. Always use the lowest absorbency that lasts, since higher absorbencies dry the vaginal wall and increase risk. Cups and discs can generally be worn up to twelve hours. Reusable items must be washed with plain soap and thoroughly dried; cups should be boiled for a few minutes between cycles.

Genital hygiene needs less intervention than the market implies. The vagina is self-cleaning and maintains an acidic pH near 3.8 to 4.5 through resident lactobacilli. Douching, scented washes and internal deodorants disturb that ecology and are associated with bacterial vaginosis rather than protecting against it. Washing the external vulva with warm water, changing products regularly, and wearing breathable underwear covers essentially all genuine hygiene need.
ingredients: Absorbent pads in at least two absorbencies, plus panty liners for the tail end of a period; the most useful single item to stock deeply because they need no washing facilities.
Tampons in regular and super, if used; buy the lowest absorbency that lasts four to eight hours rather than the highest available.

A medical-grade silicone menstrual cup or disc, sized by the manufacturer's guidance; a twelve-hour wear time makes this the most practical option where washing water is scarce but scrupulous hand hygiene is possible.
Reusable cloth pads or absorbent underwear, which need washing but no resupply, and are the sensible core of a long-term preparedness store.
A simple analgesic that blocks prostaglandins — ibuprofen or naproxen — kept where it will actually be reached on day one, plus paracetamol as an alternative for those who cannot take NSAIDs.
A hot water bottle, chemical heat pad or adhesive heat patch, which trials place roughly on a par with ibuprofen for cramp relief.
Dark spare underwear, a sealable bag for used or soiled items, and unscented soap; scented washes and douches disturb vaginal flora and should be avoided.
Iron-rich foods or, if a clinician has confirmed deficiency, an iron supplement, since regular menstruation adds roughly a milligram per day to iron requirements.

sections.heading: When Something Is Wrong: The Common Named Conditions
sections.body:
Several distinct conditions present through the cycle, and knowing their signatures shortens the path to diagnosis considerably.

Polycystic ovary syndrome is the commonest endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women, affecting roughly 8 to 13 percent. Diagnosis under the widely used Rotterdam criteria requires two of three features: infrequent or absent ovulation, clinical or biochemical excess androgens such as hirsutism or raised testosterone, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. The core disturbance involves insulin resistance and raised LH driving ovarian androgen production, which impairs follicle selection so that many small follicles persist and none becomes dominant. It presents as long or absent cycles, acne, unwanted hair, difficulty conceiving, and often weight gain, and it carries long-term metabolic and endometrial risks that make it worth treating even when fertility is not a concern.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, affecting around 10 percent of reproductive-age women. That tissue responds to cyclical hormones, bleeds, and provokes inflammation, adhesions and scarring. The characteristic picture is pain that starts before bleeding and outlasts it, deep pain during intercourse, painful bowel movements or urination around periods, chronic pelvic pain and subfertility. Crucially, the extent of disease correlates poorly with the severity of pain. Diagnostic delay averaging seven to ten years remains common.

Adenomyosis is the related condition in which endometrial tissue grows into the muscular uterine wall, producing a bulky, tender uterus, heavy bleeding and severe cramping, most often in people in their forties who have had children.

Uterine fibroids are benign smooth-muscle tumours affecting a large fraction of women by age 50, more commonly and more severely in women of African ancestry. Those distorting the cavity cause heavy or prolonged bleeding; larger ones cause pressure, urinary frequency and abdominal enlargement.

Absent periods have their own differential. Primary amenorrhoea means no menarche by 15, or by 13 with no pubertal development. Secondary amenorrhoea means three months without a period in someone previously regular, or six in someone previously irregular. Pregnancy is always the first thing to exclude. Beyond that, functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea from low energy availability — commonly below about 30 kilocalories per kilogram of fat-free mass per day — overtraining or psychological stress is very common and is a diagnosis of exclusion. Thyroid disease in either direction, raised prolactin from a pituitary adenoma or certain drugs, and primary ovarian insufficiency all need testing.

Finally, unexplained heavy bleeding since menarche should prompt screening for an inherited bleeding disorder, most often von Willebrand disease, which is present in a meaningful minority of such cases and is routinely missed.

Two further causes are common and easily tested. Thyroid dysfunction alters cycles in both directions: an underactive thyroid tends to produce heavy, frequent bleeding and can raise prolactin, while an overactive one produces light or absent periods. Structural lesions of the cavity — endometrial polyps and submucosal fibroids — typically cause bleeding between periods or after sex, and are found by ultrasound or hysteroscopy. A written record of several cycles — dates, duration, protection changes and pain scores — changes a consultation far more than any account given from memory.

sections.heading: Modifying the Cycle: Contraception, Treatment and Honest Uncertainty
sections.body:
The cycle can be deliberately altered, and understanding how clarifies what these interventions do and do not do. Combined hormonal contraception — pills, patches and rings containing an oestrogen and a progestin — works chiefly by suppressing the GnRH pulse generator so that FSH and LH never rise enough to select a dominant follicle or trigger an LH surge. Ovulation therefore does not occur; the endometrium stays thin, and cervical mucus stays hostile. The bleed that occurs in the hormone-free week is a withdrawal bleed, not a menstrual period: it is lighter, it reflects no ovarian event, and there is no medical necessity for it. Skipping it by running packets continuously is safe for most users and is standard practice for managing endometriosis, heavy bleeding and menstrual migraine.

Progestin-only methods act differently depending on dose and route. The levonorgestrel intrauterine system works mainly locally, thinning the endometrium so profoundly that bleeding is reduced by around 80 to 90 percent, which makes it a first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding as well as a contraceptive; many users become amenorrhoeic, and ovulation often continues. Implants and injectables suppress ovulation more consistently but produce unpredictable bleeding patterns, which is the commonest reason for discontinuation.

Non-hormonal medical options exist and are underused. Tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic taken only on bleeding days, reduces menstrual blood loss by roughly a third to a half by counteracting the plasmin that keeps menstrual blood liquid. NSAIDs reduce loss by perhaps 20 to 40 percent while also treating pain. Surgical options range from endometrial ablation through fibroid removal to hysterectomy, and are reserved for defined indications.

It is worth being candid about the limits of current knowledge, because this field is genuinely under-researched relative to its prevalence. The causes of premenstrual dysphoric disorder are not settled. Why endometriosis develops in some people and not others is unresolved, with retrograde menstruation clearly insufficient as an explanation since it occurs in most women. The popular claim that cohabiting people synchronise their cycles has not survived careful re-analysis and is best regarded as an artefact of overlapping variable cycle lengths. Claims that athletic performance varies dramatically and predictably by cycle phase are widely repeated but rest on small, heterogeneous studies; the current best summary is that any average effect is small and that individual variation dominates. Fertility apps predicting ovulation from calendar data alone are frequently wrong.

The practical stance that follows is to track your own data rather than trust population averages, to treat persistent deviation from your own pattern as a reason to seek assessment, and to insist on a mechanism-based explanation for symptoms rather than accepting that they must simply be endured.

guides.safetyNote: This is general education, not a substitute for individual medical care. Seek urgent attention for: bleeding that soaks through a pad or tampon every hour for two or more consecutive hours; sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain, especially with a missed period or a positive pregnancy test, which can indicate an ectopic pregnancy; fainting; or the sudden onset of high fever, vomiting, a sunburn-like rash, dizziness and confusion while using a tampon or cup, which may be toxic shock syndrome — remove the device and seek emergency care immediately. Arrange a non-urgent appointment for periods that have stopped for three months without pregnancy, for pain that stops you working or is not relieved by over-the-counter analgesia, and for bleeding between periods or after sex.

guides.title: Planning a Healthy Pregnancy
guides.summary: A comprehensive guide to preparing for pregnancy and carrying it safely: how conception works, what to fix before you conceive, nutrition and supplements, medicines and exposures to avoid, screening, age and fertility, and what to do when things go wrong.

sections.heading: Why the Months Before Conception Matter Most
sections.body:
Most people picture pregnancy care as something that begins when a test turns positive. Biologically, that is late. By the time a home pregnancy test detects human chorionic gonadotropin in urine, usually around the day of a missed period, the embryo is already about four weeks along by the conventional dating system and has been implanted in the uterine lining for roughly a week. The neural tube, the structure that becomes the brain and spinal cord, closes between days 21 and 28 after fertilisation, which is often before a person has any reason to suspect they are pregnant. The heart begins beating around day 22. The limb buds appear in week five. In other words, the entire period of most intense organ formation, called organogenesis, overlaps almost exactly with the window in which a pregnancy is easiest to miss.

This timing has a hard practical consequence. Interventions that protect the embryo during organogenesis only work if they are already in place at conception. Folic acid supplementation is the clearest example: it reduces neural tube defects substantially when started at least one month before conception, and does very little if started at eight weeks. The same logic applies to switching a teratogenic medicine to a safer alternative, achieving stable blood glucose in diabetes, treating an underactive thyroid, updating vaccinations that cannot be given during pregnancy, and stopping alcohol. Each of these is a preconception task, not a prenatal one.

There is a second, less obvious reason to plan. Roughly forty per cent of pregnancies worldwide are unplanned, and unplanned pregnancies are systematically more likely to begin with unaddressed risks: an unmanaged chronic condition, an unrecognised medication exposure, ongoing smoking or drinking, or a nutritional deficiency. Planning does not merely add benefits; it removes a set of avoidable harms that cluster together.

Finally, planning creates the space to make decisions calmly that are difficult to make under time pressure. Genetic carrier screening, for instance, is far more useful before conception, when the full range of options remains open, than at eleven weeks. Financial arrangements, parental leave, housing, and the honest question of whether both partners actually want a child now are all easier to discuss without a due date bearing down.

The reasonable target is a window of about three months of deliberate preparation, which happens to match the roughly seventy-four days it takes a sperm cell to mature and the several months over which the ovarian follicle destined to be released has been developing. Neither gamete is made overnight, and neither is a body ready to support a pregnancy. Three months is not a magic number, and starting one month out is far better than not starting at all, but it is a realistic runway for fixing most of what can be fixed.

sections.heading: How Conception Actually Works
sections.body:
Understanding the mechanics of conception makes the rest of pregnancy planning intelligible rather than a list of rules. A typical menstrual cycle runs 21 to 35 days and is conventionally counted from the first day of full bleeding, which is day one. The first phase, the follicular phase, is the variable one: it is where cycles get longer or shorter. During it, follicle-stimulating hormone from the pituitary gland recruits a cohort of ovarian follicles, of which one usually becomes dominant. That follicle produces rising oestrogen, which thickens the uterine lining and, past a threshold sustained for a day or two, flips the pituitary's response from negative to positive feedback. The result is a surge of luteinising hormone, and roughly 24 to 36 hours after that surge begins, the follicle ruptures and releases an egg. This is ovulation.

The second phase, the luteal phase, is comparatively fixed at about 12 to 16 days in most people, averaging 14. The collapsed follicle becomes the corpus luteum and secretes progesterone, which converts the uterine lining into a receptive, secretory surface and raises core body temperature by roughly 0.3 to 0.5 degrees Celsius. If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum involutes after about two weeks, progesterone falls, and the lining is shed. Because the luteal phase is the stable part, ovulation in a 35-day cycle happens around day 21, not day 17.

The fertile window is short and asymmetric. The released egg is viable for only about 12 to 24 hours. Sperm, protected in the crypts of the cervix by fertile-type mucus, can survive up to five days, occasionally a little longer. The practical fertile window is therefore about six days, ending on the day of ovulation, with the highest per-cycle probability of conception from intercourse on the two days before ovulation and on the day itself. Intercourse the day after ovulation contributes almost nothing.

Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer third of the fallopian tube. The fertilised egg divides as it travels, reaching the uterus as a blastocyst around day five or six, and implants roughly six to ten days after ovulation. Implantation is when the developing placenta first secretes human chorionic gonadotropin, the hormone home tests detect.

Even under ideal conditions, a healthy couple in their twenties has only about a 20 to 30 per cent chance of a clinically recognised pregnancy in any given cycle. Cumulatively, around 85 per cent conceive within twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse. Knowing this baseline prevents a great deal of unnecessary alarm after two or three unsuccessful months, and it explains why the standard definition of infertility waits a full year before applying at all.

sections.heading: Timing Intercourse and Tracking Ovulation
sections.body:
If conception is a matter of hitting a six-day window, the obvious question is how to find it. Several methods exist, and they differ sharply in accuracy, cost and the burden they impose. The simplest approach, and the one most fertility specialists actually recommend for the first several months, is not to track at all: have intercourse every two to three days across the cycle. This guarantees that sperm are present whenever ovulation occurs, without requiring anyone to interpret a chart. It also avoids the well-documented psychological cost of scheduled, obligatory sex, which is a real and underrated source of relationship strain.

For those who want more precision, calendar estimation is the crudest method. Subtract 14 from the usual cycle length to approximate the ovulation day, then treat the preceding five days as fertile. It is only reliable in cycles that are genuinely regular, and it fails badly in cycles that vary by more than a few days.

Cervical mucus observation is free, requires no equipment, and predicts ovulation prospectively rather than confirming it afterwards. Under rising oestrogen, mucus changes from scant and tacky to abundant, clear, slippery and stretchy, often compared to raw egg white. The last day of that fertile-quality mucus, the so-called peak day, correlates closely with ovulation. Basal body temperature, taken with a sensitive thermometer immediately on waking before rising, shows a sustained rise of 0.3 to 0.5 degrees Celsius after ovulation. Its weakness is fundamental: it confirms ovulation only after the fertile window has already closed, so it is useful for learning the shape of your cycles across several months but useless for timing intercourse in the current one.

Urinary luteinising hormone tests, sold as ovulation predictor kits, detect the LH surge and typically give one to two days of warning. Testing once or twice daily from around cycle day ten, or earlier in short cycles, is usual. Their limitations are worth knowing: polycystic ovary syndrome can produce chronically elevated LH and repeated false positives, an LH surge does not always result in an actual egg release, and some people have a surge brief enough to fall between once-daily tests.

Two persistent myths deserve dismissal. Position during or after intercourse has no demonstrated effect on conception; sperm reach the cervical mucus within minutes and are not meaningfully influenced by gravity. Second, abstaining for long stretches to build up sperm does not help and can hurt, since prolonged abstinence increases DNA fragmentation in sperm. Ejaculation every two to three days is close to optimal. Standard vaginal lubricants, including saliva and most water-based commercial products, can impair sperm motility in laboratory testing; if lubricant is needed, use a fertility-friendly, non-spermicidal formulation, or mineral oil, which appears neutral.

Whichever method is chosen, keep a simple written record of the first day of each period for several months. Cycle length and its variability are the single most informative pieces of data a clinician can be handed, and they cost nothing to collect.

sections.heading: The Preconception Visit: What to Actually Ask For
sections.body:
A preconception consultation is one of the highest-value medical appointments available, and one of the least used. It is a single visit, typically 20 to 30 minutes, ideally three to six months before you intend to conceive, and it has a definite agenda rather than being a general check-up. Booking it explicitly as a preconception visit rather than turning up and mentioning it in passing makes a considerable difference to what gets covered.

The history is the substance of the visit. Expect questions about menstrual pattern and any previous pregnancies including miscarriages, terminations and complications; existing diagnoses, particularly diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, thyroid disease, autoimmune conditions, asthma and mental health conditions; every prescription, over-the-counter product, herbal remedy and supplement currently taken; alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and other drug use; occupational and household exposures; immunisation status; family history on both sides including birth defects, intellectual disability, inherited conditions and consanguinity; and previous abdominal or pelvic surgery. Bring an actual written list of medicines and doses; recalling them accurately in a consultation room is harder than it sounds.

Laboratory work is usually modest. A full blood count identifies anaemia and, with red cell indices, can raise suspicion of thalassaemia trait. Blood group and rhesus D status matter because a rhesus-negative person carrying a rhesus-positive fetus may need anti-D immunoglobulin. Rubella immunity is checked because rubella infection in the first trimester causes severe congenital defects and the vaccine is a live vaccine that cannot be given during pregnancy. Varicella immunity is checked for the same reason. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and syphilis serology are standard, since all four are transmissible to the fetus and all four have interventions that dramatically reduce that risk. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is checked where there is a history or symptoms, and increasingly as a matter of routine. Where diabetes risk exists, glycated haemoglobin gives a three-month average of blood glucose.

Certain findings change the plan entirely rather than merely adding a note. A glycated haemoglobin above roughly 6.5 per cent means conception should reasonably be deferred until glucose control improves, because the risk of congenital malformation rises steeply with periconceptional hyperglycaemia. An untreated overactive or underactive thyroid should be corrected first. A medicine such as isotretinoin, sodium valproate, warfarin or an ACE inhibitor needs a planned substitution well in advance.

Ask three specific questions before you leave. First: given my history, is there anything I should change or start now, before conceiving? Second: are any of my current medicines a problem in pregnancy, and if so what is the alternative and when should we switch? Third: is there anything in my or my partner's family history that warrants genetic counselling? Those three questions capture most of the value of the visit even if the consultation is rushed.

sections.heading: Folic Acid, the Neural Tube, and Other Supplements
sections.body:
Folate is a B vitamin required for one-carbon metabolism, the chemistry that supplies methyl groups for DNA synthesis and repair. Rapidly dividing tissue is exquisitely dependent on it, and no tissue divides faster than an early embryo. When folate is insufficient during the closure of the neural tube, between days 21 and 28 after fertilisation, the tube can fail to close, producing anencephaly at the cranial end or spina bifida further down. The evidence here is unusually strong for a nutritional intervention: the British Medical Research Council's randomised trial, published in 1991, found that 4 milligrams of folic acid daily reduced recurrence of neural tube defects by about 72 per cent in women who had already had an affected pregnancy. Population-level flour fortification, adopted in the United States in 1998 and in many countries since, produced measurable falls in prevalence.

The standard recommendation for people without special risk factors is 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, started at least one month before conception and continued through the first twelve weeks. A higher dose, usually 5 milligrams daily in the United Kingdom or 4 milligrams in the United States, is advised for a defined higher-risk group: a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, diabetes, a body mass index above 30, epilepsy treated with certain anticonvulsants, coeliac disease or other malabsorption, sickle cell disease, or a family history of neural tube defects. Do not improvise a high dose by taking multiple multivitamins, because that also multiplies the vitamin A content, which carries its own risk.

Vitamin D is the other supplement with broad support: 10 micrograms, equivalent to 400 international units, daily, and more where deficiency is documented or likely, which includes darker skin, limited sun exposure, covering clothing and higher latitudes in winter. Iodine is required for fetal thyroid hormone synthesis and hence brain development; requirements rise by roughly 50 per cent in pregnancy, and people who avoid dairy, fish and iodised salt are at genuine risk. Iron is not universally needed before conception but should be corrected if ferritin or haemoglobin is low, since starting pregnancy iron-depleted almost guarantees anaemia later.

The most important caution runs the other way. Retinol, the preformed animal form of vitamin A, is teratogenic in high doses. Avoid supplements containing retinol and avoid liver and liver products such as pâté, which can contain extraordinary concentrations. Beta-carotene, the plant precursor, is not a concern. High-dose herbal preparations should generally be stopped, not because all are harmful but because most are simply untested in pregnancy, and an unknown risk with no known benefit is a poor trade. A standard pregnancy-formulated multivitamin is a reasonable single product for anyone who finds separate supplements unmanageable.

sections.heading: Nutrition, Body Weight and Metabolic Readiness
sections.body:
Nutrition before conception operates through two channels: supplying specific nutrients the embryo needs, and setting the metabolic environment in which it develops. The second is easy to underestimate. Maternal insulin resistance, chronic low-grade inflammation and excess adiposity change the intrauterine environment in ways associated with neural tube defects, congenital heart disease, macrosomia, gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth and caesarean delivery. These associations are consistent across large cohorts, though establishing strict causation for each is harder than the headline numbers suggest.

Body mass index gives a rough but useful frame. The range associated with the fewest complications is roughly 18.5 to 24.9 kilograms per square metre. Above 30, risks rise progressively; a body mass index above 40 roughly triples the odds of gestational diabetes compared with the normal range. Below 18.5, risks also rise, with a stronger association with low birth weight, preterm birth and, at very low weights, absent ovulation. The honest framing is that even modest change helps: a 5 to 10 per cent reduction in body weight measurably improves ovulatory function and insulin sensitivity, and there is no requirement to reach an ideal number before conceiving. What is not advisable is aggressive dieting during pregnancy itself, which is why weight change belongs in the preconception window.

The dietary pattern with the best evidence is unglamorous and familiar: abundant vegetables and fruit, whole grains rather than refined, legumes, nuts, fish, olive oil, moderate dairy, limited red and processed meat, and limited added sugar. Mediterranean-pattern diets have been associated with lower rates of gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia in randomised and observational work. Protein should be adequate, around 1.0 to 1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight daily. Long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid, matter for fetal brain and retinal development; two portions of fish weekly, one of them oily, is the usual target.

Fish carries a genuine trade-off, since methylmercury accumulates up the food chain and is neurotoxic to the developing brain. The practical rule is to eat plenty of low-mercury fish, such as salmon, sardines, herring, trout and most shellfish, and to avoid the high-mercury predators: shark, swordfish, king mackerel, marlin and tilefish. Tuna occupies a middle position, with limits usually set around two portions of light tinned tuna weekly and much less for fresh or albacore.

Caffeine deserves a specific number rather than vague advice. Most authorities cap intake at 200 milligrams daily during pregnancy, roughly one strong filter coffee or two mugs of instant, counting tea, cola, energy drinks and dark chocolate. Above that, observational data associate higher intake with miscarriage and lower birth weight, although confounding by nausea, which both reduces coffee intake and marks a healthier pregnancy, complicates interpretation.

sections.heading: Managing Chronic Conditions Before You Conceive
sections.body:
A chronic condition is not a reason to avoid pregnancy; it is a reason to plan one deliberately. The general principle is that a condition should be stable, on a pregnancy-compatible treatment, for a defined period before conception, and that the disease itself is usually a greater threat to the pregnancy than well-chosen treatment.

Diabetes is the clearest case. Elevated glucose during organogenesis is directly teratogenic, and the risk of major congenital malformation scales with glycated haemoglobin. At a value near the normal range the excess risk is small; at 10 per cent or above it may exceed 10 per cent of pregnancies. Most guidance recommends aiming below 6.5 per cent before conception where achievable without severe hypoglycaemia, along with high-dose folic acid, retinal and kidney assessment, and a review of oral agents. Metformin and insulin are generally continued; several other agents are not.

Hypertension raises the risk of pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction and placental abruption. The critical preconception task is switching drug classes. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers cause fetal kidney damage, skull hypoplasia and oligohydramnios when used in the second and third trimesters, and should be replaced, typically with labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa. Epilepsy demands the same forward planning. Sodium valproate carries roughly a 10 per cent risk of major congenital malformation and a substantially higher risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and is avoided in anyone who might become pregnant wherever an alternative exists. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have more reassuring profiles. Seizures themselves are dangerous, so stopping medication unilaterally is the wrong response; the change must be planned with a neurologist months ahead, since dose adjustment and monitoring take time.

Thyroid disease is easy to overlook and easy to fix. Maternal thyroxine is essential for fetal brain development in the first trimester, before the fetal thyroid functions. Requirements rise by 25 to 50 per cent early in pregnancy, so many people on levothyroxine need a dose increase as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, often arranged in advance as a standing instruction. Autoimmune conditions such as lupus and inflammatory bowel disease are best conceived into during remission; active disease predicts worse outcomes than most of the drugs used to control it. Hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine and sulfasalazine are generally continued; methotrexate and mycophenolate are strongly teratogenic and require a washout period, three months for methotrexate in most guidance.

Asthma should be optimised rather than reduced. Poorly controlled asthma harms the fetus through hypoxia far more than inhaled corticosteroids do, and inhalers are continued throughout pregnancy. The single sentence that captures the whole area is this: do not stop a medicine because you are pregnant or planning to be. Ask first, plan the substitution, and change it under supervision.

sections.heading: Medicines, Chemicals and Environmental Exposures
sections.body:
A teratogen is any agent capable of causing a structural or functional defect in a developing embryo or fetus. Their behaviour follows recognisable rules. Effect depends on timing: exposure in the first two weeks after conception tends to be all-or-nothing, either killing the conceptus or leaving it unaffected, because cells at that stage are still totipotent. From weeks three to eight, during organogenesis, exposure produces structural malformations, and which organ is affected depends on what is forming that week. After week eight the risk shifts from gross malformation to growth restriction and functional impairment, particularly of the brain, which continues developing to term and beyond. Effect also depends on dose, on genetic susceptibility, and on whether the agent crosses the placenta.

Some medicines are established human teratogens and must be avoided or substituted. Isotretinoin, used for severe acne, causes a characteristic pattern of craniofacial, cardiac and central nervous system defects at ordinary therapeutic doses, which is why prescribing programmes mandate contraception and pregnancy testing; a one-month washout is usually specified. Thalidomide, the historical case that created modern drug regulation after roughly 10,000 affected births between 1957 and 1962, causes limb reduction defects. Warfarin causes nasal hypoplasia and skeletal abnormalities in the first trimester and fetal bleeding later. Sodium valproate, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, methotrexate and mycophenolate belong on the same list. Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy on theoretical grounds.

A great many medicines, however, are used safely, and the reflex to stop everything causes real harm. Paracetamol, most penicillins and cephalosporins, many antihistamines, inhaled asthma treatments, levothyroxine, insulin, and several antidepressants including sertraline are all used in pregnancy. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen are a middle case: generally avoided from 20 weeks because of effects on fetal kidney function and amniotic fluid, and after 30 weeks because they can close the ductus arteriosus prematurely.

Household and occupational exposures matter less than most people fear, with specific exceptions. Lead crosses the placenta freely and impairs neurodevelopment; sources include old paint disturbed by renovation, some traditional cosmetics and remedies, and certain glazed ceramics. Organic solvents used without ventilation, pesticide application, ionising radiation above diagnostic levels, and anaesthetic gas scavenging failures are the classic occupational concerns; healthcare, agriculture, printing, painting and manufacturing warrant a specific conversation with an occupational health service. Toxoplasma is acquired from cat faeces and undercooked meat, so delegate litter tray cleaning or use gloves, and garden with gloves. Diagnostic radiography of the chest or a limb delivers fetal doses far below the threshold associated with harm, and necessary imaging should not be refused out of vague fear; the calculation for abdominal computed tomography is different and should be made explicitly.

sections.heading: Alcohol, Tobacco, Cannabis and Other Drugs
sections.body:
Alcohol crosses the placenta freely, and fetal blood alcohol concentration approaches maternal levels within minutes. The fetal liver has minimal capacity to metabolise it, and alcohol persists in amniotic fluid, effectively re-exposing the fetus. The damage is dose-related but the mechanism operates across a spectrum: at high and particularly binge-pattern exposure it produces fetal alcohol syndrome, characterised by a specific facial pattern of short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum and a thin upper lip, growth restriction, and central nervous system dysfunction. At lower exposures the structural signs may be absent while the neurodevelopmental effects, grouped as fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, remain. There is no reliably established safe threshold, and no safe trimester, because the brain develops throughout. The consistent recommendation is abstinence during pregnancy and while trying to conceive. This is a genuine case where the evidence for low-level exposure is uncertain, and the guidance is precautionary rather than proof of harm at one drink; the honest statement is that harm at low doses has not been excluded.

Tobacco acts by different mechanisms. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin, reducing oxygen-carrying capacity, and nicotine causes vasoconstriction of the uteroplacental vessels. The result is chronic relative hypoxia. Smoking roughly doubles the risk of low birth weight, raises the risk of placental abruption and placenta praevia, increases preterm birth, and is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for sudden infant death syndrome, along with cleft lip and palate. Quitting at any stage helps, and quitting before conception or in the first trimester restores much of the birth-weight difference. Nicotine replacement therapy is considered preferable to continued smoking by most authorities, on the reasoning that it removes carbon monoxide and thousands of combustion products; vaping is less studied and is not established as safe, though it is likely less harmful than smoking. Second-hand smoke exposure carries measurable risk of its own.

Cannabis is common and frequently assumed harmless. Tetrahydrocannabinol crosses the placenta and binds cannabinoid receptors that are active in fetal neurodevelopment. Cohort studies associate prenatal exposure with lower birth weight and with attention and behaviour differences in childhood, though disentangling tobacco co-use and socioeconomic confounding is genuinely difficult. Potency has risen substantially, so older reassuring studies may not describe current products. The reasonable position is that it is not established as safe and should be avoided.

Opioids, stimulants and other drugs each carry specific risks, but the dominant practical issue is that abrupt withdrawal can itself be dangerous. Opioid dependence in pregnancy is managed with maintenance treatment such as methadone or buprenorphine rather than detoxification, because withdrawal is associated with fetal distress and relapse. Neonatal abstinence syndrome is anticipated and treated. The overriding message is to disclose use honestly to a clinician; the alternative, concealment, produces far worse outcomes than the drug itself in many cases.

sections.heading: Vaccination and Infection Prevention
sections.body:
Several infections that are trivial in adults are devastating to a fetus, and the interventions against them mostly belong before conception rather than during pregnancy. The governing rule is that live attenuated vaccines are avoided in pregnancy on theoretical grounds, so they must be given beforehand, while inactivated vaccines are safe and some are actively recommended during pregnancy.

Rubella is the historical driver of this whole area. Maternal infection in the first trimester causes congenital rubella syndrome, with deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects and intellectual disability, at rates approaching 85 per cent when infection occurs before eleven weeks. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is live, so immunity should be confirmed by serology and, if absent, the vaccine given with a recommended interval before conception, commonly stated as one month. Varicella follows the same logic: chickenpox in pregnancy risks congenital varicella syndrome and severe maternal pneumonia, and the vaccine is live.

Some vaccines are given during pregnancy rather than before. Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended in any trimester, because pregnancy substantially increases the risk of severe influenza and because maternal antibody crosses the placenta and protects the newborn during the months before they can be vaccinated. Pertussis vaccine, given as a combined preparation in the late second or third trimester, is one of the clearest successes in modern obstetrics: infant whooping cough is dangerous in the first weeks of life and maternal immunisation provides passive protection precisely then. Respiratory syncytial virus vaccination in late pregnancy has been added in several countries for the same reason.

Infections not covered by vaccination require behavioural control. Listeria monocytogenes grows at refrigerator temperatures and causes miscarriage, stillbirth and neonatal sepsis, which is the reason for avoiding unpasteurised dairy, soft mould-ripened and blue cheeses, pâté, cold cured meats and pre-prepared salads, and for reheating leftovers thoroughly. Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from undercooked meat, unwashed produce and cat faeces; the practical measures are cooking meat through, washing produce, gardening with gloves and delegating litter trays. Cytomegalovirus is the commonest congenital infection in high-income countries and there is no vaccine; the main reservoir is the saliva and urine of toddlers, so handwashing after nappy changes and not sharing food, cutlery or dummies with young children are the meaningful precautions, particularly for nursery and childcare workers.

Sexually transmitted infections deserve deliberate screening rather than assumption. Untreated syphilis causes stillbirth and congenital syphilis, and is entirely curable with penicillin. HIV transmission from mother to child can be reduced from roughly 25 per cent to under 1 per cent with antiretroviral therapy, delivery planning and infant prophylaxis. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea cause neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia and are linked to preterm birth. Hepatitis B transmission is largely preventable with neonatal vaccination and immunoglobulin. Every one of these has a large intervention effect, which is exactly why the screening panel exists.

sections.heading: Genetic Carrier Screening and Family History
sections.body:
Most inherited conditions relevant to reproduction are autosomal recessive: a person carrying one altered copy of a gene and one normal copy is entirely healthy, but if both parents carry an alteration in the same gene, each pregnancy has a one in four chance of inheriting two altered copies and being affected. Because carriers are healthy, family history frequently gives no warning at all. This is why screening exists as a population offer rather than being reserved for those with an affected relative.

Carrier frequencies are higher than people expect. Roughly one in 25 people of northern European ancestry carries a cystic fibrosis variant. Sickle cell trait affects around one in 12 African Americans. Beta thalassaemia trait is common around the Mediterranean, the Middle East, South Asia and Southeast Asia. Tay-Sachs, Canavan disease and several others are enriched in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, historically screened as a panel. Spinal muscular atrophy carrier frequency is about one in 50 across many groups. Ancestry-based screening was the traditional model; expanded carrier screening, which tests hundreds of genes at once regardless of background, is increasingly offered and sidesteps the growing inaccuracy of self-reported ancestry in mixed populations.

Sequence matters. Screening one partner first is cheaper and usually sufficient, since a negative result in one partner makes an affected child very unlikely for a recessive condition; only if that partner screens positive is the other tested. Doing it before conception rather than during pregnancy is the substantive point, because it preserves options that later disappear: in vitro fertilisation with preimplantation genetic testing, use of donor gametes, adoption, prenatal diagnosis with a fully considered plan, or a decision to accept the risk knowingly. None of those are decisions to make at eleven weeks under time pressure.

Family history should be collected systematically over three generations on both sides. The findings that should prompt referral to a genetic counsellor are specific: a known inherited condition; two or more miscarriages; a stillbirth or neonatal death; a child or close relative with a birth defect, intellectual disability or developmental delay; early-onset cancer clusters; consanguinity, meaning parents who are related, which raises the chance both carry the same rare recessive variant; or ancestry from a population with a recognised founder condition. Advanced paternal age, generally above 40 to 45, modestly raises the rate of new dominant mutations, a different mechanism from the maternal-age chromosomal risk.
