Screening has real limits that should be stated plainly. A negative result reduces risk but never eliminates it, because no panel covers every variant of every gene. Results can be ambiguous, reported as variants of uncertain significance, which are genuinely difficult to act on. And results carry implications for siblings and existing children, which some people would rather not know. Counselling before testing, not only after, is what makes the process useful rather than merely alarming.

sections.heading: Age, Fertility Decline and Realistic Expectations
sections.body:
Female fertility declines with age through a mechanism that is well understood and cannot presently be reversed. Unlike sperm, which are produced continuously, oocytes are made once. A female fetus has around six to seven million oocytes at twenty weeks of gestation, about one to two million at birth, and roughly 300,000 to 400,000 at puberty. From then, follicles are lost continuously through atresia, with only about 400 ever ovulated across a reproductive lifetime. The decline in quantity accelerates after about age 37. Quality declines in parallel and matters more: the chance that an oocyte carries a chromosomal abnormality, most often from errors in meiotic segregation of chromosomes held in arrest for decades, rises steeply with age.

The numbers are worth stating concretely, while remembering that they are population averages and say nothing definite about an individual. Monthly conception probability is roughly 20 to 25 per cent in the early twenties, around 15 per cent at 35, and under 5 per cent at 40. The risk of trisomy 21 at birth is approximately one in 1,500 at age 20, one in 900 at 30, one in 350 at 35, one in 100 at 40, and about one in 30 at 45. Miscarriage rates follow the same curve, from roughly 10 to 12 per cent in the twenties to 25 per cent at 40 and above 50 per cent past 45, driven mainly by aneuploidy. Rates of gestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders, placenta praevia, caesarean delivery and stillbirth all rise with maternal age, though the absolute risks in a healthy 38-year-old remain modest.

Ovarian reserve testing, using anti-Müllerian hormone and antral follicle count on ultrasound, measures how many follicles remain. It predicts response to fertility drugs reasonably well, which is its legitimate clinical use. It is a poor predictor of natural fertility, and a low result in someone conceiving naturally should not be read as a verdict. This distinction is frequently blurred in commercial testing marketing.

Male fertility declines too, more gradually. Semen volume, motility and normal morphology decline from around age 40, DNA fragmentation rises, and the rate of new mutations in sperm increases with each paternal year, contributing to a small absolute rise in achondroplasia, Apert syndrome and possibly autism and schizophrenia. Time to conception lengthens measurably when the male partner is over 45.

The practical response is not panic but arithmetic. If you want two or three children and are 36, the timeline is different from wanting one at 30. Oocyte cryopreservation is a genuine option, most effective when performed before 35, with success falling sharply after 38; it should be presented honestly, since per-oocyte live birth rates mean a meaningful number of stored eggs is required.

sections.heading: The Male Partner: Sperm Health and Shared Responsibility
sections.body:
Roughly 40 to 50 per cent of infertility involves a male factor, either alone or alongside a female factor, yet preconception advice is still routinely addressed only to the person who will carry the pregnancy. This is both unfair and clinically wrong. Sperm production, spermatogenesis, takes about 74 days from stem cell to mature spermatozoon, with a further two weeks or so of maturation in the epididymis. That means changes made today alter the sperm being ejaculated in roughly three months, which is precisely why the three-month preconception window applies to both partners.

The testes sit outside the body because spermatogenesis requires a temperature about two to four degrees Celsius below core temperature. Anything that defeats that arrangement reduces sperm production: frequent hot baths and saunas, prolonged laptop use directly on the lap, extended driving without breaks, and, more importantly than most realise, obesity, which insulates the scrotum and also converts testosterone to oestrogen in adipose tissue. Varicocele, a dilated network of scrotal veins present in around 15 per cent of men and up to 40 per cent of those with infertility, raises scrotal temperature and is potentially correctable surgically.

Smoking reduces sperm count, motility and normal morphology and increases DNA fragmentation. Heavy alcohol use suppresses testosterone and impairs sperm production. Anabolic steroids are a common and under-disclosed cause of profound suppression, since exogenous testosterone shuts down the pituitary signals that drive spermatogenesis; recovery after stopping takes many months and is occasionally incomplete. Some prescription medicines matter too, including sulfasalazine, certain calcium channel blockers, spironolactone, chemotherapy agents and finasteride. Cannabis affects motility. Heat, toxins, radiation and pesticide exposure at work are all documented contributors.

Diet and body composition matter in the expected direction. Antioxidant-rich diets, adequate zinc, selenium and folate, regular moderate exercise, and normalising body weight all show modest improvements in semen parameters. The evidence for antioxidant supplements specifically is mixed and often based on small trials; a reasonable position is that a good diet is well supported while expensive supplement stacks are not.

Semen analysis is the diagnostic test, and it should be requested early rather than after a year of investigating the female partner alone. It is cheap, non-invasive and informative. Current World Health Organization reference values, revised in 2021, place the fifth-centile thresholds at approximately 1.4 millilitres volume, 16 million sperm per millilitre, 39 million total sperm, 42 per cent total motility, 30 per cent progressive motility and 4 per cent normal forms. These are reference limits from men whose partners conceived within a year, not sharp cut-offs between fertile and infertile; a result slightly below one threshold is not a diagnosis. Because counts vary considerably, an abnormal result should be repeated after about three months before conclusions are drawn.

sections.heading: Mental Health, Stress, Sleep and Practical Support
sections.body:
Mental health is not a soft addendum to pregnancy planning. Perinatal mental illness affects roughly one in five women, suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in the year after birth in several high-income countries, and untreated maternal depression is itself associated with preterm birth, low birth weight and impaired mother-infant interaction. The preconception period is when medication decisions should be made calmly rather than during a first-trimester crisis.

The central dilemma is real and should not be resolved by reflex. Untreated illness carries risk; medication carries risk; and the relevant comparison is between them, not between medication and an imaginary risk-free state. Most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have been extensively studied, with sertraline often preferred; paroxetine has been associated with a small absolute increase in cardiac defects in some studies, an association that has weakened as confounding by indication has been better controlled. Late-pregnancy exposure can produce a transient neonatal adaptation syndrome, usually mild and self-limiting. Lithium requires specialist supervision because of a rare association with Ebstein's anomaly and because blood levels shift with pregnancy physiology. Sodium valproate is contraindicated when used as a mood stabiliser in anyone who might conceive. Abruptly stopping an effective antidepressant on discovering a pregnancy carries a high relapse rate and is generally the worst available option.

Certain histories predict risk strongly enough to justify a plan made in advance. A previous episode of postpartum psychosis carries a recurrence risk of roughly 50 per cent, which makes prophylactic treatment and an agreed monitoring plan a reasonable proposal. Bipolar disorder, previous severe depression, a history of trauma or previous traumatic birth, and eating disorders all warrant a named clinician and a written plan before conception rather than a referral made at 30 weeks.

Ordinary stress is a different question and is frequently over-blamed. There is no good evidence that everyday stress prevents conception, and telling someone struggling to conceive to relax is both unkind and unsupported. Severe, chronic stress does affect the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and can disrupt ovulation, and there is a plausible association between very high stress and preterm birth, but the everyday version does not deserve the guilt attached to it.

Sleep is more actionable than it appears. Short sleep and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea are associated with gestational diabetes and hypertensive disorders, and both are more treatable before pregnancy than during it. Shift work, particularly rotating nights, is associated in cohort data with menstrual irregularity and modestly increased miscarriage risk.

Practical support belongs in the same conversation. Establish who will help in the first six weeks after birth, what parental leave both partners are entitled to and how it will be split, how the household finances absorb reduced income, and whether housing is adequate. Screening for domestic abuse belongs here too, because pregnancy is a recognised period of escalation rather than protection.

sections.heading: The Positive Test and the First Twelve Weeks
sections.body:
Home pregnancy tests detect the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin in urine. Sensitive tests detect concentrations around 20 to 25 international units per litre, which is typically reached about 12 to 14 days after ovulation, or around the day of a missed period. Testing earlier produces false negatives because implantation may not yet have occurred; the advice to retest in three days after a negative result with a missed period is sound. False positives are uncommon but occur after a recent miscarriage, with certain fertility drugs containing hCG, and rarely with some tumours.

Dating uses the first day of the last menstrual period, which places the notional start of pregnancy about two weeks before conception. Naegele's rule gives an estimated due date by adding one year and seven days to that date and subtracting three months. Only about 4 per cent of babies arrive on that exact day, and an ultrasound between 8 and 13 weeks dates the pregnancy more accurately than any calendar calculation, particularly in irregular cycles.

Bleeding in early pregnancy is common, occurring in around a quarter of pregnancies, and roughly half of those continue normally. It nonetheless always warrants assessment, because the alternative diagnoses matter. Ectopic pregnancy, where implantation occurs outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube, occurs in about 1 to 2 per cent of pregnancies and is a genuine surgical emergency; the classic presentation is one-sided lower abdominal pain with bleeding around six to eight weeks, and shoulder-tip pain or faintness suggests intra-abdominal bleeding requiring immediate care.
steps: Confirm with a home urine test from the first day of a missed period; if negative but the period does not arrive, repeat in three days using first-morning urine, which is most concentrated.

Start or continue 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, or the higher 5 milligram dose if you fall into a high-risk group, plus 10 micrograms of vitamin D, and continue folic acid to the end of week twelve.
Stop alcohol entirely, stop smoking and vaping, cap caffeine at 200 milligrams daily, and stop any non-essential supplement containing retinol.

Contact a midwife or doctor within the first week to book antenatal care; in many systems the first booking appointment is targeted at 8 to 10 weeks and access to screening depends on booking promptly.
List every medicine you take and ask specifically whether each should be continued, substituted or stopped, and do not discontinue anything before that conversation.
Record the first day of your last menstrual period and your usual cycle length, since both are needed for dating before an ultrasound is available.
Arrange the dating and nuchal translucency ultrasound, usually offered between 11 weeks 2 days and 14 weeks 1 day, and decide in advance whether you want combined or cell-free DNA screening.
Seek same-day assessment for heavy bleeding, one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, fever above 38 degrees Celsius, or severe persistent vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down.

sections.heading: When It Does Not Go to Plan
sections.body:
Most pregnancy planning guidance implicitly assumes success within a few months, which leaves people unprepared for the two commonest outcomes that are not that: taking longer than expected, and losing a pregnancy. Both are far more usual than public conversation suggests, and both have a defined path forward.

On timing, the benchmark is that about 85 per cent of couples having regular unprotected intercourse conceive within twelve months, and roughly half of the remainder conceive in the following year without treatment. Infertility is conventionally defined as failure to conceive after twelve months, reduced to six months when the female partner is over 35 and to immediate assessment where there is an obvious cause such as absent or very irregular periods, known tubal disease, previous pelvic infection or surgery, endometriosis, chemotherapy exposure, or a known male factor. Waiting the full year in those situations wastes time that is not recoverable.

Initial investigation is straightforward and should proceed in parallel for both partners rather than sequentially. It typically comprises semen analysis, confirmation of ovulation with a mid-luteal progesterone measured about seven days before the expected period, assessment of tubal patency by hysterosalpingography or laparoscopy, a pelvic ultrasound, and hormonal tests including thyroid function and, where polycystic ovary syndrome is suspected, androgens. Treatment depends entirely on the cause: ovulation induction with letrozole or clomifene, surgery for tubal or endometriotic disease, intrauterine insemination, or in vitro fertilisation with or without intracytoplasmic sperm injection. Success rates fall sharply with female age and should be requested as age-specific live-birth rates per cycle started, not as pregnancy rates per embryo transfer, which flatter the figures considerably.

Miscarriage occurs in roughly 10 to 20 per cent of clinically recognised pregnancies and in a much higher proportion of all conceptions, many of which are never detected. Around half to two-thirds result from chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, which are random events, not consequences of anything the parents did. Lifting, exercise, sex, stress, minor falls and working do not cause miscarriage, and it is worth saying so directly, because unwarranted self-blame is close to universal. Recurrent miscarriage, usually defined as two or three consecutive losses, justifies investigation for antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine structural abnormalities, thyroid disease, poorly controlled diabetes and parental chromosomal rearrangements; even after full investigation, around half of cases have no identified cause, and the prognosis for a subsequent pregnancy remains reasonably good.

Grief after early loss is frequently unrecognised by others, who may not have known about the pregnancy at all. It is a real bereavement, not a disappointment, and the absence of ritual or acknowledgement makes it harder rather than easier. Seeking support is proportionate. So is deciding, after due consideration, to stop trying; that is a legitimate outcome and not a failure of planning.

guides.safetyNote: This guide is general education, not personal medical advice. Pregnancy decisions depend on your individual history, and some situations are emergencies: heavy vaginal bleeding, severe one-sided abdominal or shoulder-tip pain in early pregnancy (possible ectopic pregnancy), a severe headache with visual changes or upper abdominal pain after 20 weeks (possible pre-eclampsia), fever above 38 C, or reduced fetal movement after 28 weeks all warrant urgent assessment rather than waiting. Never start or stop a prescribed medicine on the strength of a written guide.
